items.title: Accounting standards, Ind AS and the form of the statements
items.core_explanation_md:
**Accounting standards** set out how to **recognise, measure, classify, present and disclose** transactions. Their aim is to **reduce alternatives**, give **comparability** between enterprises and give users **meaningful information**.

| Body | Role |
| --- | --- |
| **Accounting Standards Board** (set up by ICAI) | Formulated the Accounting Standards |
| **IASB** | Develops **IFRS** |
| **ICAI** | Recommends standards to the **NFRA** |
| **Ministry of Corporate Affairs** | **Notifies** the standards |

**Ind AS** is India's adaptation of IFRS, changed to fit the Indian economic and legal setting. If an **Act conflicts** with an Ind AS, the **Act prevails**.

**Form (courseware account):** formats of the balance sheet and profit and loss account are in the Act, except for **insurance, banking, electricity** and companies under other laws. The statements must give a **true and fair view**, comply with the standards and **disclose any deviation**, its reasons and financial effect. The accounting year ends on **31 March**, and every company must prepare statements **even if there is no activity**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Dates and thresholds for Ind AS applicability are not taught here because they were not checked against a current source.

self_check.prompt_text: If an Act and an Ind AS conflict, which prevails?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The provision of the Act, to the extent of the conflict.

items.title: Balance sheet: current and non-current
items.core_explanation_md:
A **balance sheet** is a **snapshot** of what the entity **owns (assets)** and **owes (liabilities)** at a date, which it must state.

| | **Current** if | Otherwise |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Asset** | Realised, sold or consumed in the **normal operating cycle**; or **held for trading**; or realised **within 12 months** after the reporting date; or **cash or cash equivalent** (unless restricted for at least 12 months) | **Non-current** |
| **Liability** | Settled in the **normal operating cycle**; or **held for trading**; or due **within 12 months**; or the company has **no unconditional right to defer** settlement for 12 months | **Non-current** |

A **trade receivable** is due for **goods sold or services rendered in the normal course of business**; a **trade payable** is due for **goods or services bought** in the normal course.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Current versus non-current drives the liquidity ratios you will use later.

self_check.prompt_text: A loan due for repayment in nine months. Current or non-current?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Current, because it is due within twelve months of the reporting date.

items.title: The balance sheet format
items.core_explanation_md:
**Equity and liabilities**

1. **Shareholders' funds:** share capital; reserves and surplus; money against share warrants
2. **Share application money pending allotment**
3. **Non-current liabilities:** long-term borrowings; deferred tax liabilities (net); other long-term liabilities; long-term provisions
4. **Current liabilities:** short-term borrowings; trade payables; other current liabilities; short-term provisions

**Assets**

1. **Non-current assets:** fixed assets (tangible, intangible, capital work-in-progress, intangible assets under development); non-current investments; deferred tax assets (net); long-term loans and advances; other non-current assets
2. **Current assets:** current investments; inventories; trade receivables; cash and cash equivalents; short-term loans and advances; other current assets

**Notes worth a banker's attention:** secured versus unsecured **borrowings**; trade receivables **outstanding more than six months**; **goods in transit** within inventories; **contingent liabilities** (claims not acknowledged as debt, guarantees, other) and **commitments**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Contingent liabilities are not on the balance sheet total but may become real obligations.

self_check.prompt_text: Under which head do trade payables appear?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Current liabilities.

items.title: The statement of profit and loss
items.core_explanation_md:
| Step | Item |
| --- | --- |
| I | **Revenue from operations** |
| II | **Other income** |
| III | **Total revenue** = I + II |
| IV | **Expenses:** materials consumed, purchases of stock-in-trade, changes in inventories, employee benefits, **finance costs**, **depreciation and amortisation**, other expenses |
| V | **Profit before exceptional and extraordinary items and tax** = III - IV |
| | Adjust for **exceptional** and **extraordinary** items to get **profit before tax** |
| | Deduct **tax** (current and deferred) to get **profit from continuing operations** |
| | Add **discontinuing operations** (after tax) to get **profit for the period** |
| | **Earnings per share:** **basic** and **diluted** |

**Finance costs:** interest expense, other borrowing costs, net foreign exchange gain or loss.

**Other income:** interest income (non-finance company), dividend income, net gain or loss on sale of investments, other non-operating income.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The extraordinary items line follows the courseware format; check the current Schedule III for its use.

self_check.prompt_text: What is total revenue in this format?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Revenue from operations plus other income.

items.title: The cash flow statement
items.core_explanation_md:
The **cash flow statement (CFS)** follows **cash and cash equivalents** over the period:

**Opening cash + sources of cash - uses of cash = Closing cash**, which must equal the cash in the second balance sheet.

**Cash** = cash on hand and **demand deposits** with banks. **Cash equivalents** = **short-term, highly liquid** investments readily convertible into cash **without significant erosion in value**.

| Component | Content |
| --- | --- |
| **Operating** | Cash from and for running the business; should be **positive** for the company to **stay solvent** |
| **Investment** | **Long-term** receipts and payments not from operations (capital and debt transactions excluded) |
| **Financing** | Transactions in **capital and debt** |

**What the lender learns:** whether **profit and net cash flow agree**, whether accrual income is **actually turning into cash**, and whether the business can meet **sure, timely outflows** such as an ad hoc loan repayment or retiring a usance letter of credit.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A profitable company can still run out of cash; the CFS shows that.

self_check.prompt_text: Which of the three cash flows should be positive for the company to remain solvent?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Operating cash flow.

items.title: The funds flow statement
items.core_explanation_md:
Compare **two balance sheets**. Each change in an item (other than cash) is a **source** or a **use** of funds:

| Change | Source or use |
| --- | --- |
| **Increase** in a **liability** | **Source** |
| **Decrease** in an **asset** | **Source** |
| **Increase** in an **asset** | **Use** |
| **Decrease** in a **liability** | **Use** |

The statement shows what happened to the excess of **long term sources over long term uses**, that is, to **net working capital**. If **more is used long term than raised long term**, net working capital **falls**: the funds have been **diverted** (for example, short term money financing long term assets).
items.expanded_explanation_md: Net working capital = current assets less current liabilities.

self_check.prompt_text: A company raises a new term loan. Source or use?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A source, because a liability has increased.

items.title: Projected financial statements
items.core_explanation_md:
Past statements show what happened. To judge **how much credit is needed** and **whether the activity will pay**, the banker needs the **future** position, so **projected statements** are used.

| Case | How the projection is made |
| --- | --- |
| **Working capital** | Anticipate the **level of operations** and project assets and liabilities, using past statements as the guide |
| **New enterprise** (no past statements) | Prepare on an assumed **level of activity** |
| **Smaller enterprise** (little financial expertise) | Often prepared **by the bank**, by **interviewing** the borrower |
| **Term loan** (new project or expansion) | Cover the **whole loan period**, to test **viability** and set the **disbursal and repayment schedule** |

Projections **given by the borrower** are examined **critically for reasonableness**; if they look unreasonable, the bank **discusses** and reaches a **consensus** with the borrower.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The banker never takes a projection at face value: reasonableness is tested against the past record.

self_check.prompt_text: For a term loan to a new project, how long should the projected statements run?
self_check.expected_takeaway: For the entire duration of the bank loan.

items.title: Why bankers analyse: six purposes
items.core_explanation_md:
| | Purpose | What the banker does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a | **Performance and financial position** | Study growth and profit **trend**, industry comparison, asset/liability mix, **leverage**, profit retention |
| b | **Future performance** | Project earnings prospects and growth from the past |
| c | **Danger signals** | Spot deterioration early and take **preventive** steps |
| d | **Credit requirement** | Assess the need accurately: **over-financing** and **under-financing** are both risky; judge repayment, credit risk and terms |
| e | **Funds flow** | Confirm bank funds were used for the **intended purpose**, no **diversion**, no unacceptable liquidity mismatch from short-term sources |
| f | **Cross checking** | Compare the **stock and book debt statements** for **drawing power** with the **balance sheet** (use the nearest date if there is none for the balance sheet date) |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Different users look for different things: an investor may care about earnings per share, a tax authority about turnover, a banker about repayment.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is over-financing a risk to the bank as well as to the borrower?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It lets funds be diverted or idle and weakens repayment prospects; the courseware calls both over- and under-financing risky for borrower and bank.

items.title: Rearranging the balance sheet: sources and uses
items.core_explanation_md:
The credit officer regroups the balance sheet into **short-term** and **long-term** blocks:

| | **Sources (liabilities)** | **Uses (assets)** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Short term** | **Current liabilities**: working capital finance availed from the bank, and other current liabilities | **Total current assets (TCA)** |
| **Long term** | **Term liabilities** + **net worth** (paid-up capital, reserves and surplus) | **Fixed assets**, other non-current assets, intangible assets |

**Net working capital (NWC)** = the surplus of **long-term sources over long-term uses** = **current assets - current liabilities**.

For net worth, **tangible net worth** is net worth less **intangible assets**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: When NWC is positive, part of the current assets is financed by long-term money.

self_check.prompt_text: What are the two equal ways to compute NWC?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Long-term sources minus long-term uses, or current assets minus current liabilities.

items.title: Rearranging the profit and loss account and what to adjust
items.core_explanation_md:
**CMA-style layout** (the old Credit Monitoring Arrangement format, still a useful guide):

1. **Gross sales**; less GST/VAT/duty = **net sales**
2. **Cost of sales**: raw materials, power and fuel, direct labour, other manufacturing expenses, depreciation, **add opening stocks, less closing stocks**
3. **Selling, general and administrative expenses**
4. = **Operating profit**
5. less **interest** = operating profit after interest
6. add **non-operating income**, less **non-operating expenditure**
7. = **PBT**; less **tax** = **PAT**

**Checklist when rearranging** (adjust where needed): term loan instalments **due within one year** (treat as **current** liabilities); advance tax and tax provision; **deferred tax**; **non-moving inventory**; receivables **over six months old**; **revaluation** and **intangibles**; **investments and loans to associates and subsidiaries**; bills purchased or discounted; **contingent liabilities**; provisioning; **depreciation method**; **inventory valuation**; **expenses of earlier years**; **events after the accounting period**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Each item on the checklist can change the profit or the net worth the banker works with.

self_check.prompt_text: How is a term loan instalment due within one year treated for analysis?
self_check.expected_takeaway: As a current liability.

items.title: Funds flow analysis by the banker
items.core_explanation_md:
The three methods bankers mostly use: **funds flow analysis**, **trend analysis** and **ratio analysis**.

**Funds flow statement:** not part of the financial statements and **not certified by the auditor**; it is a **lender's requirement** to **trace diversions**. Borrowers give it in the **CMA** model; if not, the banker **prepares it from the last two balance sheets**, grouping total sources and total uses into **long term** and **short term**.

**Reading it:** if **long-term uses exceed long-term sources** (that is, short-term sources are financing long-term uses), working capital funds have been **diverted** and the matter needs **probing**.

**Not every diversion is bad:** a company with a **very high current ratio** may use idle funds to add capacity. The **guiding principle**: the diversion must **not push liquidity below the desired level**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Use the NWC idea: NWC falls when long-term uses exceed long-term sources.

self_check.prompt_text: Is a diversion of funds always a warning sign?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No, it may be sensible if liquidity stays at the desired level, for example with a very high current ratio.

items.title: Trend analysis and common size statements
items.core_explanation_md:
**Trend analysis**

- Arrange the items **vertically**: actuals of **two past years**, **this year's estimate**, **next year's projection**.
- Show the **percentage increase or decrease over the previous year** beneath each figure.
- Use it for **sales, operating profit, PBT, PAT** and for **balance sheet items**.

**Common size statements** express each item as a **percentage of one key figure** (for example raw material consumption as a percentage of sales).

- Percentages put figures on a **common base**, so **companies of different sizes** can be compared.
- They let an analyst compare **operating and financing characteristics** of two firms in the same industry.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Trend asks "which way is it moving?"; common size asks "how does the cost structure compare?".

self_check.prompt_text: Raw material consumed is Rs 60 lakh on sales of Rs 200 lakh. What is the common size figure?
self_check.expected_takeaway: 30 per cent of sales.

items.title: Ratio analysis and liquidity ratios
items.core_explanation_md:
A **ratio** compares two figures. It can be shown as a **percentage** (23.7 per cent), a **number** (current ratio 1.33) or a **proportion** (debt equity 1:2). The two figures can come from the **profit and loss account**, the **balance sheet**, or one of each.

| Ratio | Formula | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Current ratio** | **TCA / total current liabilities** | **Liquidity**; normally benchmarked at **1.33 : 1** (the 0.33 is the NWC cushion) |
| **NWC ratio** | **NWC / TCA x 100** | Share of current assets financed by **long-term sources** |
items.expanded_explanation_md: A current ratio of 1.33 means NWC is one quarter of TCA, so the NWC ratio is 25 per cent.

self_check.prompt_text: At a current ratio of 1.33, what share of TCA is financed by long-term sources?
self_check.expected_takeaway: About 25 per cent (0.33 / 1.33).

items.title: Profitability ratios
items.core_explanation_md:
| Ratio | Formula (as the courseware defines it) | Tells you |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Raw material to cost of production** | RM consumed / cost of production x 100 | Sensitivity to **raw material price** |
| **PBT ratio** | PBT / net sales x 100 | **Profitability efficiency** |
| **PAT ratio** | PAT / net sales x 100 | Owners' **earnings share** of sales |
| **EBITDA margin** | EBITDA / net sales x 100 | **Operating performance** |
| **ROCE** | EBITDA / total of the asset side x 100 | **Operating performance** against capital used |
| **Operating profit ratio** | Operating profit / net sales x 100 | True **business profitability** (non-operating items removed) |

**EBITDA** = PAT + interest + depreciation + tax + amortisation.

The **Internal Rate of Return (IRR)** is the **discount rate that makes the NPV of all future cash flows from an investment zero**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware itself says ROCE is defined differently by different authors; use the formula the question gives.

self_check.prompt_text: Which profit measure does the operating profit ratio leave out?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Non-operating income and non-operating expenses.

items.title: Leverage (solvency) ratios
items.core_explanation_md:
| Ratio | Formula | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **TOL / TNW** | **Total outside liabilities** / **tangible net worth** | **TOL** = term liabilities + current liabilities; **TNW** = net worth - intangible assets; shown as **times** |
| **TOL / Adjusted TNW** | TOL / (TNW - loans, advances and investments in **group, associate, subsidiary** companies) | More **conservative**: such money has gone out of the system and risk may be shared across entities |
| **Debt equity (project)** | **Debt component** / **margin component** of the means of finance | A plain ratio |
| **Debt equity (company)** | **Long term debt / net worth** (analysts also use TOL / net worth) | Solvency indicator |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Lower is safer: it means the owners have put in more of their own money relative to outside liabilities.

self_check.prompt_text: Why deduct loans to group companies in adjusted TNW?
self_check.expected_takeaway: That money has left the borrower for related entities and cannot absorb its losses.

items.title: Debt service coverage ratio
items.core_explanation_md:
The **DSCR** tests ability to **service term debt out of future earnings**.

| Variant | Formula |
| --- | --- |
| **Net DSCR** | **Cash accrual** / **instalments of all term loans due** in the period |
| **Gross DSCR** | **(Cash accrual + interest on term loans)** / **(instalments due + interest on term loans)** |

**Cash accrual** = **net profit + non-cash expenses** (such as depreciation).

Why gross DSCR adds interest to both: **interest also has to be paid**, so it belongs in the **denominator**; and since **net profit is struck after deducting interest**, it is **added back** to the numerator so that the test is of **repayment ability**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Net DSCR tests instalments only; gross DSCR tests instalments plus interest.

self_check.prompt_text: Which variant of DSCR puts interest into the denominator?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The gross DSCR.

items.title: Other coverage ratios
items.core_explanation_md:
| Ratio | Formula | Reading |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Vanquish ratio** | **Long term debt / EBITDA** | **Years** to wipe off long term debt at today's EBITDA |
| **Interest coverage ratio** | **EBITDA / interest on all borrowings** | **Times** earnings cover interest |
| **Fixed asset coverage ratio (FACR)** | **WDV of fixed assets under charge / term loans outstanding** | **Times** the debt is secured by fixed assets |
| **Security margin coverage ratio** | **(WDV of FA - term loans outstanding) / WDV of FA x 100** | **Cushion** of security, in per cent |
items.expanded_explanation_md: FACR and the security margin ratio use the same numbers; one is in times and the other is the margin in per cent.

self_check.expected_takeaway: 3 years.

items.title: Holding (turnover) ratios and the deficiencies of ratio analysis
items.core_explanation_md:
**Holding ratios** show the **operating cycle** and the **working capital gap** (TCA - OCL).

| Holding | Formula | Base |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Raw material** | Average RM stock / RM consumed x 365 | Consumption |
| **Stock in process** | Average SIP / cost of production x 365 | Cost of production |
| **Finished goods** | Average FG stock / cost of sales x 365 | Cost of sales |
| **Receivables** | Average debtors / **gross** sales x 365 | Gross sales (debtors owe tax too) |
| **Payables** | Average creditors / purchases x 365 | Purchases |

**Amount from days:** holding days x (base / 365) = the amount held. The four **asset** holdings add up to **TCA**; payables give **sundry creditors** (part of OCL). Use **12** instead of 365 to get **months**.

**Inventory turnover** = **net sales / average inventory**; higher means **faster** movement.

**Deficiencies:** the P&L covers a **period** but the balance sheet a **date**, so an **average** is used, which does not cure **seasonal** swings or year-end **bunching** of sales; the **current ratio can be doctored** on the balance sheet date. Ratios remain the best available tool.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The holding ratios turn the operating cycle into rupees of working capital.

self_check.prompt_text: Why do receivable holdings use gross sales rather than net sales?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because the debtors' balance includes the tax element (GST or VAT) and so relates to gross sales.

items.title: Creative accounting
items.core_explanation_md:
**Creative accounting** is dressing up the facts and figures: **window dressing**. The practitioner usually **plays with the rules rather than breaking them**.

- **Not all creative accounting is fraud**, but **most frauds involve it**.
- **A common method:** booking **advances received from customers for future sales** as **current year income**. This **inflates** turnover, profit and net worth and **improves** profitability, liquidity, gearing, coverage and receivable holding ratios, while **understating** current liabilities and TOL and **distorting** income tax and GST liability.

**How a credit officer spots it**

- read the **notes on accounting policies** and **between the lines**;
- watch for a **change of statutory or independent auditors** with **no statutory reason**;
- look **beyond the printed balance sheet**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Detecting it is a test of the credit officer's vigilance.

self_check.prompt_text: Which side of the balance sheet is understated when advances from customers are booked as income?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Liabilities: current liabilities and so total outside liabilities are understated.

items.title: Related party transactions
items.core_explanation_md:
A **related party transaction** is a **transfer of resources, services or obligations** between a reporting entity and a related party, **whether or not a price is charged** (Ind AS 24, as the courseware quotes it).

**A person (or close family member) is related if they:** have **control or joint control**, have **significant influence**, or are **key management personnel** of the entity or its parent.

**An entity is related if it is:** in the **same group**; an **associate or joint venture** of the other; **joint ventures** of the same third party; a **post-employment benefit plan** for either entity's employees; or **controlled or significantly influenced** by an identified person.

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Control** | Power to govern **financial and operating policies** to get benefits |
| **Joint control** | **Contractually agreed** sharing of control |
| **Key management personnel** | Those with **authority and responsibility** for planning, directing and controlling |
| **Significant influence** | Power to **participate** in policy decisions **without control** |

**Not related merely because of:** a **common director**; **shared joint control**; normal dealings with **lenders, trade unions, public utilities, government departments**; or a **customer, supplier, franchisor, distributor or agent** with a large volume of business (**economic dependence**).
items.expanded_explanation_md: Why bankers care: most creative accounting, diversion and siphoning happens through related party transactions, so they must be examined carefully.

self_check.prompt_text: Are two companies related parties just because they share a director?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No: a common director or key management member alone does not make them related parties.

items.title: Priority sector: farm credit limits
items.core_explanation_md:
**Individual farmers** (and their SHGs/JLGs, and proprietorship firms of farmers) can get priority sector credit for crop loans, medium and long-term loans, pre- and post-harvest activities, distressed farmers' debt, **Kisan Credit Card** loans, **land purchase by small and marginal farmers**, and solar pumps and solar plants on their own land.

**Produce-pledge loans** (up to 12 months): up to **Rs 90 lakh against NWR/eNWR** and **Rs 60 lakh against other warehouse receipts**.

| **Corporate farmers, FPOs/FPCs, partnership firms, farmer co-operatives** | Limit |
| --- | --- |
| Crop loans, medium/long-term loans, pre- and post-harvest loans | **Rs 4 crore** aggregate per borrowing entity |
| Produce-pledge loans (12 months) | **Rs 4 crore** (NWR/eNWR), **Rs 2.5 crore** (other receipts) |
| FPOs/FPCs farming with **assured marketing at a pre-determined price** | **Rs 10 crore** per entity |
| Purchase of **members' produce** | **Rs 10 crore** |

Urban co-operative banks **cannot** lend to co-operatives of farmers under this head.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The Rs 4 crore limit is an aggregate: several eligible loans to the same entity together cannot count beyond it.

self_check.prompt_text: A corporate farming company has crop loans of Rs 3 crore and a machinery loan of Rs 2 crore. How much counts under the Rs 4 crore aggregate limit?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Rs 4 crore at most; the excess does not qualify under that head.

items.title: Agriculture infrastructure, ancillary services and small and marginal farmers
items.core_explanation_md:
| Head | Limit |
| --- | --- |
| **Agriculture infrastructure** | **Rs 100 crore** per borrower from the banking system |
| **Food and agro-processing** | **Rs 100 crore** per borrower from the banking system |
| **Start-ups** in agriculture and allied services | **Rs 50 crore** |

**Who counts as a small or marginal farmer (SMF)**

- **Marginal:** landholding **up to 1 hectare**
- **Small:** **more than 1 and up to 2 hectares**
- **Landless** agricultural labourers, tenant farmers, oral lessees and share-croppers, within SMF limits
- **SHGs/JLGs** of SMFs (disaggregated data kept)
- Individuals **solely in allied activities**, loans up to **Rs 2.5 lakh**, with no land criterion
- **FPOs, FPCs and farmer co-operatives** where the **SMF landholding share is at least 75 per cent**, within the Rs 4 crore and Rs 10 crore farm credit limits
items.expanded_explanation_md: SMF loans count towards the 10 per cent SMF sub-target and also qualify as weaker section lending.

self_check.prompt_text: A farmer holds 1.6 hectares. Marginal or small?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A small farmer (more than 1 and up to 2 hectares).

items.title: MSME, export credit and education under priority sector
items.core_explanation_md:
**MSME:** **all bank loans** to MSMEs qualify, plus start-ups that meet the MSME definition (up to **Rs 50 crore**). Also eligible: **with-recourse factoring** for an MSME assignor, factoring through **TReDS**, **Khadi and Village Industries** units (micro), producers' co-operatives in the decentralised sector, loans to MFIs for on-lending, and loans to registered NBFCs for on-lending to micro and small enterprises up to **Rs 20 lakh** per borrower. **PMJDY overdrafts** count as micro enterprise lending.

**Export credit** (other than agriculture and MSME):

| Bank type | Eligible |
| --- | --- |
| Domestic banks, WoS of foreign banks, SFBs, UCBs | **Incremental** export credit up to **2 per cent** of ANBC or CEOBSE (the higher), with **Rs 50 crore** per borrower |
| Foreign banks, **20 branches and above** | **2 per cent**, no per-borrower limit |
| Foreign banks, **fewer than 20 branches** | Export credit up to **32 per cent** of ANBC or CEOBSE (the higher) |

**Education:** loans to individuals, including vocational courses, up to **Rs 25 lakh**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Export credit to agriculture or MSMEs is counted in those categories instead, under their own limits.

self_check.prompt_text: Which type of bank may count export credit up to 32 per cent of ANBC?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A foreign bank with fewer than 20 branches.

items.title: Housing loans under priority sector
items.core_explanation_md:
A housing loan to an individual qualifies only if it meets **both** the **loan limit** and the **dwelling unit cost limit** for the **population of the centre**:

| Centre population | Loan limit | Max cost of dwelling unit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **50 lakh and above** | Rs **50** lakh | Rs **63** lakh |
| **10 lakh to below 50 lakh** | Rs **45** lakh | Rs **57** lakh |
| **Below 10 lakh** | Rs **35** lakh | Rs **44** lakh |

**Repairs** to damaged dwellings: loan up to Rs **15 / 12 / 10** lakh in the three bands, within the same cost limits.

**Not eligible:** housing loans to the bank's **own employees**; loans backed by **long-term bonds** exempt from ANBC.

**Also eligible:** loans to **governmental agencies** for dwelling units or slum clearance (carpet area up to **60 sq.m.**), and **affordable housing projects** using at least **50 per cent of FAR/FSI** for dwelling units of carpet area up to 60 sq.m.

Use **Census 2011 Table A-04** population for the centre; **villages and rural areas** use the **below 10 lakh** band.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Both tests must be met: a Rs 40 lakh loan on a Rs 60 lakh flat in a 20-lakh city fails the cost test.

self_check.prompt_text: A Rs 40 lakh loan on a flat costing Rs 60 lakh in a city of 20 lakh people: eligible?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No: the cost exceeds the Rs 57 lakh limit for that band, although the loan is within Rs 45 lakh.

items.title: MSME classification under the 2025 notification
items.core_explanation_md:
| Category | Investment in plant and machinery or equipment | Turnover |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Micro** | up to **Rs 2.5 crore** | up to **Rs 10 crore** |
| **Small** | up to **Rs 25 crore** | up to **Rs 100 crore** |
| **Medium** | up to **Rs 125 crore** | up to **Rs 500 crore** |

Set by **S.O. 1364(E) of 21 March 2025**, in force from **1 April 2025** (earlier figures: Rs 1 crore / 5 crore, 10 / 50, 50 / 250).

**Composite criterion**

- Crossing the ceiling in **either** investment **or** turnover moves the enterprise to the **next higher** category.
- It is placed in a **lower** category only if it is **below the ceilings in both**.

**Other rules**

- All units with **GSTIN under the same PAN** are **one enterprise**; investment and turnover are **aggregated**.
- Investment follows the **Income Tax Return of the previous year**; a **new** enterprise uses the promoter's **self-declaration** until 31 March of the year of its first return.
- Plant and machinery or equipment means tangible assets **other than land and building and furniture and fittings**.
- **Exports are excluded** from turnover.
- Registration on the **Udyam portal** by **self-declaration** (no documents) gives a permanent **Udyam Registration Number** and an e-certificate.
items.expanded_explanation_md: This card replaces the earlier courseware-based card: the thresholds are now checked against the Gazette notification.

self_check.prompt_text: Investment Rs 2 crore, turnover Rs 12 crore. Which category?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Small: turnover exceeds the micro ceiling of Rs 10 crore, so the enterprise moves up.

items.title: Collateral-free loans to micro and small enterprises
items.core_explanation_md:
**The mandate:** banks **must not take collateral** for loans **up to Rs 20 lakh** to **micro and small enterprise (MSE)** units. Banks are advised to give collateral-free loans up to **Rs 20 lakh** to all units financed under **PMEGP** (administered by KVIC).

**Optional extension:** on the unit's **good track record and financial position**, the bank may **raise the limit to Rs 25 lakh** under its **internal policy**. It may use **Credit Guarantee Scheme** cover where applicable.

**Voluntary pledge:** gold or silver that the borrower **pledges voluntarily** for a loan within the collateral-free limit is **not a violation**.

**From when:** loans to MSE borrowers **sanctioned or renewed on or after 1 April 2026**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The earlier limit was Rs 10 lakh; the amendment doubled the mandate.

items.title: The four Labour Codes and when they took effect
items.core_explanation_md:
29 central labour laws were consolidated into **four Labour Codes**, **made effective from 21 November 2025**:

| Code | Enacted |
| --- | --- |
| **Code on Wages, 2019** | notified **8 August 2019** |
| **Industrial Relations Code, 2020** | notified **29 September 2020** |
| **Code on Social Security, 2020** | notified **29 September 2020** |
| **Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020** | notified **29 September 2020** |

**Transition:** while rules under the Codes are framed, the relevant provisions of the **existing Acts and their rules** continue in force.

**Design idea:** **single registration, single licence, single return** to cut compliance.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware says 29 labour laws were amalgamated into four Codes; the commencement date is the new fact.

self_check.prompt_text: On which date did the four Labour Codes take effect?
self_check.expected_takeaway: 21 November 2025.

citations.authority: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Labour & Employment, Government of India
citations.title: Government Makes the Four Labour Codes effective to Simplify and Streamline Labour Laws

items.title: Code on Wages, 2019
items.core_explanation_md:
**It absorbs four laws:** the Payment of Wages Act 1936, the Minimum Wages Act 1948, the Payment of Bonus Act 1965 and the **Equal Remuneration Act 1976**.

| Topic | Provision |
| --- | --- |
| **Minimum wages** | Statutory right for **all employees**, organised and unorganised (earlier about **30 per cent** of workers) |
| **Floor wage** | Set by the Government; **no State may fix minimum wages below it** |
| **Fixing wages** | By **skill level**, **area** and **job conditions** |
| **Equality** | **No discrimination on gender, including transgender identity**, in recruitment, wages and conditions for similar work |
| **Timely payment** | Applies to **all employees** (earlier only up to **Rs 24,000** a month) |
| **Overtime** | **At least twice** the normal rate |
| **Enforcement** | **Inspector-cum-Facilitator**; first-time non-imprisonable offences **compoundable**; **repeat offences within five years** not |
items.expanded_explanation_md: The Equal Remuneration Act of the courseware is therefore replaced by the equality provision in this Code.

self_check.prompt_text: Which earlier Act on equal pay is absorbed into the Code on Wages?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Equal Remuneration Act, 1976.

citations.authority: Press Information Bureau, Government of India
citations.title: India's Labour Reforms: Simplification, Security, and Sustainable Growth

items.title: Industrial Relations Code, 2020
items.core_explanation_md:
**It absorbs:** the Trade Unions Act 1926, the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act 1946 and the Industrial Disputes Act 1947.

| Topic | Provision |
| --- | --- |
| **Fixed term employment** | Full **parity in wages and benefits**; **gratuity after one year** |
| **Re-skilling fund** | **15 days' wages** per retrenched worker, **in addition to** retrenchment compensation; credited within **45 days** |
| **Union recognition** | **51 per cent** membership: **Negotiating Union**; otherwise a **Negotiating Council** from unions with **at least 20 per cent** |
| **Thresholds** | Lay-off, retrenchment, closure approval and standing orders: **100 raised to 300** |
| **Worker** | Includes supervisory employees earning up to **Rs 18,000** a month |
| **Women** | **Proportional representation in grievance committees** |
| **Disputes** | **Two-member tribunals**; direct approach after failed conciliation within **90 days** |
| **Strikes** | **14-day notice** for all establishments; **mass casual leave** counts as a strike |
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware describes industrial relations through the older Acts; this Code replaces them.

self_check.prompt_text: What notice is mandatory before a strike or lockout under the Code?
self_check.expected_takeaway: 14 days, in all establishments.

items.title: Code on Social Security, 2020
items.core_explanation_md:
**It incorporates nine Acts**, including the **Employees' Provident Funds Act 1952**, the **ESI Act 1948**, the **Maternity Benefit Act 1961** and the **Payment of Gratuity Act 1972**.

| Topic | Provision |
| --- | --- |
| **Gig and platform workers** | Defined for the first time; **aggregators contribute 1 to 2 per cent of annual turnover**, **capped at 5 per cent** of payments to such workers |
| **ESIC** | **Pan-India**; voluntary opt-in for establishments with **fewer than 10** employees |
| **Wages** | Uniform definition; **50 per cent of total remuneration** (or a notified percentage) is **added back** to compute wages |
| **Gratuity** | **Fixed-term employees** after **one year** (earlier five) |
| **Dependants** | Include **maternal grandparents**; for **female employees**, **parents-in-law** |
| **Accidents** | **Commuting accidents** between home and workplace count |
| **Fund** | **Social security fund** for unorganised, gig and platform workers |
items.expanded_explanation_md: The Code makes the wage base for gratuity and provident fund consistent across laws.

self_check.prompt_text: After how long are fixed-term employees eligible for gratuity under the Code?
self_check.expected_takeaway: After one year of continuous service.

items.title: Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020
items.core_explanation_md:
**It absorbs 13 Central Acts**, including the **Factories Act 1948**, the Mines Act 1952, the Contract Labour Act 1970 and the Building and Other Construction Workers Act 1996.

| Topic | Provision |
| --- | --- |
| **Registration** | **10 or more employees**, electronic; **one registration** instead of six |
| **Hazardous work** | Can extend to **any establishment, even one employee** |
| **Women** | May work in **all establishments** and at **night (before 6 AM, beyond 7 PM)** with **consent** and **safety measures** |
| **Employees** | **Appointment letters**; **free annual health check-up** |
| **Factories** | Threshold **10 to 20 workers** (with power), **20 to 40** (without power) |
| **Contract labour** | Threshold **20 to 50**; **all-India licence valid 5 years** |
| **Safety committees** | Establishments with **500 or more** workers |
| **Offences** | Fine-only offences compounded at **50 per cent** of the maximum fine; with imprisonment, **75 per cent** |
items.expanded_explanation_md: For a banker: night work by women in a branch or office needs consent and safety measures.

self_check.prompt_text: May women work night shifts under the OSH Code?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Yes, in all types of establishments, with their consent and required safety measures.

items.title: Working capital: gross, net and why a firm needs it
items.core_explanation_md:
Besides fixed assets, a business holds **current assets**: raw materials, work in process, finished goods and receivables. The money tied up in them is **working capital**.

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Gross (total) working capital** | The firm's **total current assets** requirement |
| **Short-term sources** | Credit from **suppliers**, other current liabilities, **bank finance** |
| **Net working capital (NWC)** | The part funded from **long-term sources**: capital or long-term borrowings |

A bank finances the **gap**: it first **assesses the current assets needed**, then expects the enterprise to bring in **some of it from its own capital or long-term money** (the NWC).
items.expanded_explanation_md: This is the same NWC as in the financial statements unit: long-term sources less long-term uses, or current assets less current liabilities.

self_check.prompt_text: What is gross working capital?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The total requirement of current assets of the enterprise.

items.title: The holding norms (operating cycle) method
items.core_explanation_md:
**Step 1 - turnover.** Existing firms: **past performance**. New firms: **production capacity, market share, raw material availability, industry norms**.

**Step 2 - gross working capital** as the sum of:

| Component | What is considered |
| --- | --- |
| **Inventory** | Raw material, work in process, finished goods: **lead time, minimum order quantity, location and number of suppliers, share of imports, process**; industry norms as a guide |
| **Receivables or bills** | **Market practice** for the business |
| **Other current assets** | Cash level, **advances to suppliers**, **advance tax** |

**Step 3 - sources:** **own NWC** (last balance sheet plus internal accruals, with extra NWC if needed for the desired current ratio), **suppliers' credit**, **other current liabilities** (salaries, expenses payable, **customer advances**).

**Bank finance = total working capital - funds from all other sources.**
items.expanded_explanation_md: The holding method is also called the operating cycle method or the traditional method.

self_check.prompt_text: How is bank finance found under the holding norms method?
self_check.expected_takeaway: As the gap between total working capital and the funds available from all other sources.

items.title: The three Tandon committee methods of lending
items.core_explanation_md:
The enterprise is required to bring in NWC as follows (the courseware says some banks still use these):

| Method | NWC the enterprise brings in |
| --- | --- |
| **First** | At least **25 per cent of the working capital gap**, where gap = total current assets - current liabilities **excluding** bank finance |
| **Second** | At least **25 per cent of total current assets** |
| **Third** | **100 per cent of core current assets** plus at least **25 per cent of the remaining** current assets |

**Resulting current ratio:** the **second** method gives **at least 1.33**; the **first** can give **less**; the **third** is likely to give **more**.

**Bank finance** = projected total current assets - stipulated NWC - projected short-term liabilities (other than bank finance).
items.expanded_explanation_md: Core current assets are the permanent minimum level of stocks and similar assets that the firm always holds.

self_check.prompt_text: Which Tandon method gives a current ratio of at least 1.33?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The second method: NWC of at least 25 per cent of total current assets.

items.title: Bank finance under the three Tandon methods
items.core_explanation_md: A firm projects total current assets of Rs 400 lakh, of which core current assets are Rs 100 lakh, and current liabilities other than bank finance of Rs 120 lakh. Find the bank finance and the current ratio under each of the three methods.

worked_steps.description: Working capital gap = current assets - other current liabilities.
First method: NWC 25 per cent of the gap; bank finance = gap - NWC.
worked_steps.intermediate_result: Bank finance Rs 210 lakh; current ratio 400 / (120 + 210) = 1.21

worked_steps.description: Second method: NWC 25 per cent of total current assets.
worked_steps.intermediate_result: Bank finance Rs 180 lakh; current ratio 400 / 300 = 1.33

worked_steps.description: Third method: NWC = core (100) + 25 per cent of the remaining 300.
worked_steps.intermediate_result: Bank finance Rs 105 lakh; current ratio 400 / 225 = 1.78

items.final_answer_with_unit: Bank finance: first Rs 210 lakh (current ratio 1.21), second Rs 180 lakh (1.33), third Rs 105 lakh (1.78)

self_check.prompt_text: Which method gives the lowest bank finance and why?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The third: it asks for the most NWC, since all core current assets are financed from long-term funds.

items.title: The cash budget method
items.core_explanation_md:
Project the firm's **cash inflows and outflows** for each month or quarter. **Bank finance = the cash deficit**, if any.

| Period line | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Receipts** | Cash from sales and other inflows |
| **Payments** | Suppliers, expenses, **interest** |
| **Surplus / deficit** | Receipts - payments |
| **Cumulative position** | Opening balance + surplus / deficit, carried forward |

The **lowest cumulative balance** is the **peak deficit** the bank finance must cover.

Why a firm needs bank finance: on some days **opening cash plus inflows** are not enough for **normal outflows**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Monthly projection is more practical than daily projection.

self_check.prompt_text: What does the peak cumulative deficit tell the banker?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The maximum bank finance needed during the period.

items.title: Projected turnover (Nayak) method and choosing a method
items.core_explanation_md:
**Projected turnover method (Nayak Committee):** the firm needs **25 per cent of annual turnover** as gross working capital: **20 per cent of turnover** from the **bank** and **5 per cent** as **margin** from the firm.

**Weakness:** it can **under-finance** units whose **working capital cycle exceeds three months**, so banks also assess on holding norms and sanction the **higher** amount.

| Method | Best suited to |
| --- | --- |
| **Holding norms** | **Uniform** operations, **stable** markets (it uses a one-year average) |
| **Cash budget** | **Large month-to-month swings**: **seasonal** industries, **project contract** execution |
| **Turnover** | **Small enterprises** without detailed records |

Holding and cash budget methods both project **activity, customer credit, supplier credit and other current items**; both depend on the **credit officer's estimates**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Details of how the turnover method is applied to micro and small enterprises are not taught here because they were not checked against a current instruction.

self_check.prompt_text: Which assessment method suits a seasonal industry?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The cash budget method.

items.title: Bills and receivables finance
items.core_explanation_md:
**Receivables finance:** the borrower gives a **statement of book debts**; the bank sets **drawing power** by deducting the **margin**.

**Bills of exchange**

| | Demand bill | Usance bill |
| --- | --- | --- |
| When | **No credit** to the buyer | **Credit** for a stated period |
| Accepted by buyer? | Not needed | **Yes**, accepted |
| Shown in seller's books as | **Book debt** (until paid) | **Bills receivable** |
| Bank action | **Collect** or **purchase** | **Discount** after deducting interest for the usance |

Bills are governed by the **Negotiable Instruments Act**, which gives **stronger legal protection** if the buyer defaults.

**Terms:** **purchase** (demand bills), **discount** (usance bills), **negotiation** (bills under an **LC** of the buyer's bank).

**Accounting and assessment:** a bill purchased, discounted or negotiated is **not an asset** of the drawer; it may be a **contingent liability** if it is not **without recourse**. For assessment, bills purchased or discounted are added to **both current assets and current liabilities** as the loan policy says; **negotiated bills are normally not added** (the counterparty is a bank and recourse is very unlikely).
items.expanded_explanation_md: The seller can receive up to 100 per cent of the bill amount on purchase, less usual charges.

self_check.prompt_text: Which kind of bill is normally "discounted"?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A usance bill.

items.title: Letters of credit, guarantees and co-acceptance: how limits are assessed
items.core_explanation_md:
**Letter of credit (LC):** the bank's undertaking, at the buyer's request, to **pay the seller against compliant documents**; governed by **UCPDC 600** (ICC publication).

**Assessing an LC limit**

1. **Amount of each LC:** from monthly consumption and the **economic order quantity (EOQ)**.
2. **Frequency:** 12 / (months of consumption in one LC).
3. **LCs outstanding at a time:** total time an LC stays outstanding (**lead time + transit + usance**) / interval between LCs, **rounded up**.
4. **LC limit** = LCs outstanding x amount of each LC.

The LC limit is normally **carved out of the fund-based limit**. A **guarantee limit** is carved out where the guarantee reduces fund-based need (for example a guarantee for **receipt of advance payment**), and a **co-acceptance limit** is carved out because **supplier credit** was not counted at assessment.

**Types of guarantee:** a **performance guarantee** protects the beneficiary against **non-performance or under-performance** of a contract; a **financial guarantee** covers **financial obligations or dues** (security deposits, earnest money, payment of dues).

**Co-acceptance:** the bank also **accepts** the bill drawn on its customer, acting as a **guarantee of payment**, so the supplier gives credit more readily.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Regulatory guidance on guarantees and co-acceptances follows in the next batch.

self_check.prompt_text: Which type of guarantee covers earnest money?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A financial guarantee.
